claims.text: Every major agent platform surveyed (Anthropic Agent Skills, LangGraph/LangChain, OpenAI Assistants + Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel, plus Perplexity's production guidance) prescribes a decision frame for when to add a new capability (tool, skill, plugin, or specialist agent).
claims.notes: Executive summary claim; cross-platform survey scope statement.

claims.text: No surveyed agent platform mandates a structured per-capability decision artifact at design time; the frames are universally prose principles rather than a fixed-shape rationale document.
claims.notes: Load-bearing negative finding for FR-7 design — explicit no-platform-mandates verdict.

claims.text: The shared substance across surveyed platforms collapses to three recurring ideas: need-justification (start simple; add only when measurably necessary), scope/lifecycle hygiene (when to use, when to stop, how it composes), and anti-pattern defenses (tool/skill proliferation degrades accuracy).
claims.notes: Tri-category convergence claim mapping onto W/H/A trifecta.

claims.text: The Why / How / Anti-patterns trifecta in FR-7 is a structural codification of community substance, not novel content; its differentiator is the mandate to write it down at design time rather than rely on prose-only principles or post-hoc eval feedback.
claims.notes: Integration/synthesis verdict claim — substance matches community; codification as mandate is novel.

claims.text: Agents demonstrably degrade in selection accuracy once tool/skill counts exceed roughly 10–20 per context.
claims.notes: Capability proliferation anti-pattern — quantified threshold. Cross-corroborated in Finding 8.

claims.text: Anthropic's official guidance for Agent Skills is discovery-driven, not specification-driven: identify capability gaps by running agents on representative tasks, then build skills incrementally to address what's missing.
claims.notes: Finding 1 — primary source: Anthropic Engineering Blog 2025-10-16.

claims.text: No fixed-shape design artifact (Why/How/Anti-patterns or equivalent) is mandated at design time for Anthropic Agent Skills.
claims.notes: Finding 1 — explicit no-mandate statement for Anthropic.

claims.text: Anthropic Agent Skills' progressive-disclosure mechanism (3-level: metadata → SKILL.md → references) is the architectural defense against context bloat, not a design rubric.
claims.notes: Finding 1 — architectural mechanism distinguished from design rubric.

claims.text: Anthropic's design discipline lives in the Skill Quality Checklist of the skill-creator skill, which lists post-hoc verification items rather than a pre-design rubric.
claims.notes: Finding 1 caveat — distinguishes post-hoc checklist from pre-design rubric.

claims.text: Perplexity's published production discipline for Agent Skills prescribes eval-first: write evals (including negative/forbidden-load examples) before authoring the skill.
claims.notes: Finding 2 — Perplexity's evals-before-skill practice. Concrete design pattern.

claims.text: Perplexity names a skill-design anti-pattern of system-prompt recapitulation: don't promote globally-relevant knowledge to a conditionally-loaded skill.
claims.notes: Finding 2 — anti-pattern #1 from Perplexity. Cross-platform anti-pattern consensus member.

claims.text: Perplexity names a skill-design anti-pattern of fast-changing remote-dependency drift: don't ship a skill that wraps an MCP endpoint whose surface mutates faster than you can maintain.
claims.notes: Finding 2 — anti-pattern #2 from Perplexity. Cross-platform anti-pattern consensus member (drift).

claims.text: Perplexity names a skill-design anti-pattern of off-target side-effects: every new skill risks degrading every existing skill.
claims.notes: Finding 2 — anti-pattern #3 from Perplexity. Cross-platform anti-pattern consensus member (off-target side effects).

claims.text: Perplexity asserts there is no first-principles answer for whether a skill is needed — only empirical inspection.
claims.notes: Finding 2 — Perplexity stance against first-principles structured-decision-frame shortcuts.

claims.text: Even Perplexity's prescription is prose-and-checklist rather than a mandated document template; the closest formal artifact is the eval suite itself.
claims.notes: Finding 2 caveat — no document template even at Perplexity.

claims.text: LangChain/LangGraph's official documentation frames tool addition as a runtime-tradeoff decision (static vs. dynamic tool sets, pre-registered vs. runtime-discovered) and warns that too many tools may overwhelm the model.
claims.notes: Finding 3 — LangChain framing.

claims.text: LangChain/LangGraph prescribes principles for tool design (clear docstrings, one-tool-one-purpose, parallel-safe marking) but mandates no design-time decision artifact.
claims.notes: Finding 3 — explicit no-mandate statement for LangGraph.

claims.text: LangGraph's `langgraph-bigtool` library — designed for agents with hundreds of tools using semantic-search retrieval — is implicit acknowledgement that the unstructured 'just bind tools' pattern breaks at scale.
claims.notes: Finding 3 caveat — architectural answer is retrieval, not design-time artifact.

claims.text: OpenAI's official orchestration guide prescribes a prose principle for adding a new specialist agent: only when capability isolation, policy isolation, prompt clarity, or trace legibility materially improves.
claims.notes: Finding 4 — OpenAI specialist-agent principle.

claims.text: OpenAI names premature specialization as an anti-pattern: splitting too early creates more prompts, more traces, more approval surfaces without quality gain.
claims.notes: Finding 4 — premature-specialization anti-pattern from OpenAI.

claims.text: OpenAI's function-calling guidance sets a soft cap of fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn, deferring the rest via tool_search.
claims.notes: Finding 4 — OpenAI 20-function soft cap. Quantified threshold.

claims.text: OpenAI's orchestration and function-calling guides mandate no structured design artifact for tool/specialist decisions.
claims.notes: Finding 4 — explicit no-mandate statement for OpenAI.

claims.text: AutoGen is in maintenance mode; new work routes to Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF).
claims.notes: Finding 5 — AutoGen successor relationship.

claims.text: Microsoft Agent Framework's workflows guide prescribes a graduated complexity ladder: single agent with tools → agents-as-tools → handoff → group chat → workflow with graph.
claims.notes: Finding 5 — MAF graduated complexity ladder. Concrete design pattern.

claims.text: Microsoft Agent Framework mandates 'use the simplest pattern that meets the requirement.'
claims.notes: Finding 5 — MAF mandate (verbatim) on the ladder.

claims.text: Microsoft Agent Framework's decision factor across the orchestration ladder is a four-way question: who decides which subtask is next, whether to involve another agent, when to ask a human, and how to handle partial failure.
claims.notes: Finding 5 — MAF four-way decision question.

claims.text: In Microsoft Agent Framework, 'the model decides' pushes toward agents-as-tools; 'the developer decides' pushes toward workflows.
claims.notes: Finding 5 — MAF decider-authority axis.

claims.text: Microsoft Agent Framework's decision frame for the orchestration ladder is prose; no mandated artifact.
claims.notes: Finding 5 — explicit no-mandate statement for MAF.

claims.text: CrewAI's official Crafting Effective Agents guide states that 80% of design effort should go into designing tasks and only 20% into defining agents.
claims.notes: Finding 6 — CrewAI 80/20 rule (verbatim).

claims.text: CrewAI prescribes 'give agents minimal tools'; overloading degrades performance.
claims.notes: Finding 6 — CrewAI minimal-tools principle.

claims.text: CrewAI's Evaluating Use Cases guide provides a Crews-vs-Flows decision matrix on complexity × precision axes — a structured decision rubric, but a runtime-architecture selector, not a per-capability rationale.
claims.notes: Finding 6 — CrewAI Crews-vs-Flows matrix. Closest cross-platform analog to structured rubric.

claims.text: CrewAI names a specific anti-pattern: a single 'research and write' agent will underperform two specialized agents.
claims.notes: Finding 6 — CrewAI's specialization anti-pattern.

claims.text: Semantic Kernel's plugin-design guidance prescribes 'import only the necessary plugins' to reduce false-positive function calls.
claims.notes: Finding 7 — Semantic Kernel less-is-more principle.

claims.text: Semantic Kernel prescribes explicit balance between single-responsibility functions (reusable but token-heavy) and multi-responsibility functions (cheaper but less reusable).
claims.notes: Finding 7 — Semantic Kernel function-granularity tradeoff.

claims.text: Semantic Kernel prescribes AI-friendly naming for plugin functions.
claims.notes: Finding 7 — Semantic Kernel naming principle.

claims.text: Semantic Kernel's October 2023 rename from Skills to plugins demonstrates that even terminology for capability-units is unsettled across the agent ecosystem.
claims.notes: Finding 7 — terminology-instability evidence.

claims.text: Semantic Kernel mandates no structured per-capability decision artifact.
claims.notes: Finding 7 — explicit no-mandate statement for Semantic Kernel.

claims.text: Multiple independent engineering blogs and pattern catalogues document the same anti-pattern: agent selection accuracy degrades sharply beyond roughly 10–20 tools per reasoning context.
claims.notes: Finding 8 — cross-platform anti-pattern consensus, 4-source corroboration (aipatternbook.com Tool Sprawl; agentpatterns.tech Too Many Tools 2026-03-16; tianpan.co Tool Explosion Problem 2026-04-13; kvg.dev Stop Drowning Your Agent in Tools 2026-01-10).

claims.text: Published thresholds indicate 5–10 tools is the practical sweet spot for agent tool selection.
claims.notes: Finding 8 — quantified sweet-spot threshold.

claims.text: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard shows isolated tool-calling at ~96% accuracy dropping to ~13–15% in large-toolset multi-turn settings.
claims.notes: Finding 8 — BFCL quantified accuracy drop.

claims.text: One widely-cited case study reports paring tools from 16 to 1 raised success from 80% to 100% with 40% lower tokens.
claims.notes: Finding 8 — case study quantification.

claims.text: The mechanism for tool-proliferation degradation is consistently described as attention dilution / context rot from tool-description token competition.
claims.notes: Finding 8 — mechanism description.

claims.text: Load-on-demand patterns (Anthropic progressive disclosure, OpenAI tool_search, LangGraph bigtool, MCP allowlist scoping) are the converging architectural defense against tool/skill proliferation.
claims.notes: Finding 8 caveat — converging architectural defense pattern.

claims.text: The closest cross-platform analog to a structured decision artifact is CrewAI's Crews-vs-Flows matrix, which is a runtime-architecture selector rather than a per-capability rationale.
claims.notes: Synthesis — structural-divergence claim about closest analog.

claims.text: The closest pre-design discipline cross-platform is Perplexity's 'write evals first' — a practice with a deliverable (the eval suite), not a document template.
claims.notes: Synthesis — closest pre-design discipline analog.

claims.text: The Why/How/Anti-patterns trifecta as a mandated, authored-at-design-time, per-capability artifact appears to be novel as a codification, even though every component of its content is well-trodden community substance.
claims.notes: Synthesis — novelty verdict for the trifecta.

claims.text: Across the surveyed sources, the same anti-patterns recur in 2024, 2025, and 2026 posts, suggesting that even teams who have read the principles continue to violate them in production.
claims.notes: Synthesis — prose-principles-produce-drift observation, motivates the trifecta mandate.

claims.text: The trifecta's contribution is forcing the rationale into a reviewable artifact, which creates an audit point so a reviewer can ask 'where's the rationale?' instead of inferring from code.
claims.notes: Synthesis — audit-point value claim.

claims.text: The trifecta concentrates the decision so that 'why-now' and 'what-could-go-wrong' sit next to each other instead of being scattered across docstrings, system prompts, and tribal memory.
claims.notes: Synthesis — concentration-of-decision value claim.

claims.text: The trifecta defends specifically against proliferation, which is the most universally-documented failure mode in the surveyed literature.
claims.notes: Synthesis — proliferation-defense value claim.

claims.text: Every surveyed platform stops short of mandating a structured form for capability decisions, suggesting the cost of the mandate (overhead, ritualistic compliance, 'filling in the boxes' without thought) is non-trivial.
claims.notes: Synthesis — trade-off about structured-vs-free-form rationale.

claims.text: The trifecta will need anti-ritualism defenses (e.g., reviewers checking substance not presence) to avoid the ritualistic-compliance failure mode.
claims.notes: Synthesis — design recommendation for anti-ritualism.

claims.text: The trifecta's Anti-patterns section should default to a curated short list with rationale rather than an exhaustive catalogue, to avoid ritual.
claims.notes: Synthesis — Anti-patterns-section design recommendation.

claims.text: Orphaned-capability decay is not named as a primary anti-pattern in the surveyed primary sources; the closest analog is Perplexity's drift-from-fast-changing-MCP-endpoint warning.
claims.notes: Open question — gap in literature about orphaned-capability decay.

claims.text: Surveyed platforms differ on what the unit of capability is (skill vs. plugin vs. function vs. specialist agent), so the trifecta's unit of mandate should be defined explicitly.
claims.notes: Open question — granularity of mandate.

claims.text: None of the surveyed sources prescribes review heuristics for capability-rationale documents, because none mandates such a document.
claims.notes: Open question — reviewer enforcement mechanics are green-field design space.
